at meditere.explanation: "At meditere" is borrowed from Latin, and the stress falls on the "-ere": med-i-TEE-re. Danish verbs ending in -ere all follow the same easy pattern: mediterer, mediterede, mediteret. The noun is "meditation", and the practice is often combined with "mindfulness", which Danes use as an English word.

sentence.en: I try to meditate every morning.

at melde sig syg.explanation: "At melde sig syg" means to call in sick, that is, to tell your work or school that you are ill and can't come. The little word "sig" turns into "mig" for yourself: "jeg melder mig syg". It describes the act of reporting, not the illness itself.

sentence.en: Today I'm calling in sick.

at mene.explanation: "At mene" means to mean or to think, and it is a bit stronger than "at synes": you hold a firm view. "Jeg mener, at du har ret" means I believe you are right. It is also used for what you intend: "Hvad mener du?" (What do you mean?). For the meaning of a word, Danish uses "at betyde".

sentence.en: What do you mean by that?

forms.en: I was allowed to / had to

at måtte.explanation: "At måtte" means to be allowed to (may) and also to have to (must). "Må jeg gå?" asks May I go?, while "Jeg må gå nu" says I have to go now. The meaning comes from the situation. In the negative, "Du må ikke" means you are not allowed to, a strong warning. It is followed straight by another action word, with no "at".

sentence.en: May I ask something?

en mail.explanation: "En mail" is the everyday short word for an email. Danes say "jeg sender en mail" far more often than the longer "e-mail". It is an en-word, so "mailen" means "the email". You can also use it as a verb, "at maile", but "at sende en mail" is the safe choice.

sentence.en: I am writing an email to the teacher.

en mand.explanation: "En mand" means a man, and also a husband when you say "min mand" (my husband). It is an en-word. The plural "mænd" has a changed vowel. Its pair is "en kvinde" (a woman) or "en kone" (a wife).

sentence.en: My husband is cooking today.

en mave.explanation: "En mave" is the stomach or belly. It is an en-word. Danes use it for both: "Jeg har ondt i maven" (My stomach hurts), and also for a round tummy. It forms "mavepine" (stomachache) and "mavesyre" (stomach acid).

sentence.en: My stomach hurts.

en mavepine.explanation: "En mavepine" is a stomachache, built from "mave" (stomach) and "pine" (pain). It is an en-word. Like with headaches, you normally say "Jeg har mavepine" without "en". A near-equal is "ondt i maven".

sentence.da: Barnet har **mavepine** og vil ikke spise.
sentence.en: The child has a stomachache and does not want to eat.

en melon.explanation: "En melon" is a melon, and it is an en-word. The word covers the whole family, so for a specific kind you say "en vandmelon" (watermelon) or "en honningmelon" (honeydew melon). It is a popular fruit in summer.

sentence.en: I buy a melon in the shop.

en menu.explanation: "En menu" is a menu, the list of food at a restaurant, and it is an en-word. You ask "kan jeg få menuen?" to get one. It can also mean a set meal, like "dagens menu" (the menu of the day), which has fixed courses for one price. Another word for the list is "et menukort".

sentence.en: Can I have the menu, please?

en meter.explanation: "En meter" is a meter, a unit of length. It is an en-word and stays the same after a number: "to meter". It is written "m". Danes use meters for height and distance, so "to meter høj" is two meters tall.

sentence.en: The house is ten meters tall.

en metro.explanation: "Metro" is the underground train, which in Denmark exists in Copenhagen. You travel "med metroen" (by the metro). It is an en-word. The S-train is a different thing, called "S-tog", so do not mix them up.

sentence.en: I take the metro to work.

en middag.explanation: "En middag" is the main hot meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening, so it is what English speakers call dinner or supper. Many Danes eat it around 18:00. Be careful: the same word can also mean noon ("midt på dagen"), but in daily talk, "middag" almost always means the evening meal, while lunch is "frokost".

sentence.en: We eat dinner at six o'clock.

en mobil.explanation: "En mobil" is what Danes call their phone in daily life. It is short for "mobiltelefon". It is an en-word, so you say "min mobil" and "mobilen". A common phrase is "Har du din mobil?" (Do you have your phone?). Many Danes also say "telefon", which means the same.

sentence.en: Where is my phone?

en mobiltelefon.explanation: "En mobiltelefon" is the full word for a mobile phone, from "mobil" (mobile) and "telefon" (phone). In daily speech Danes nearly always shorten it to "en mobil". The longer form is more common in writing, on signs and in rules like "Mobiltelefoner forbudt". It is an en-word.

sentence.en: My mobile phone is on the table.

en mor.explanation: "En mor" is a mother. When talking about your own, Danes say "min mor" with no "en". The plural "mødre" has a changed vowel. "Mor" is also used like a name when speaking to her: "Hej, mor!".

sentence.en: My mother makes good food.

en morfar.explanation: "En morfar" is your mother's father: "mor" (mother) plus "far" (father). The word for your father's father is "farfar". Note that in the plural the vowel changes, so you get "morfædre". In everyday talk the word is also used as a name for grandpa.

sentence.en: My grandfather goes for a walk every day.

en morgen.explanation: En morgen is a morning, the early part of the day. Watch out for two similar phrases: "i morgen" means tomorrow, while "i morges" means this morning. "Om morgenen" means "in the morning", for something you do regularly. It is an en-word, and "the morning" is "morgenen". "Godmorgen" is how you greet someone in the morning.

sentence.en: I drink coffee in the morning.

en mormor.explanation: "En mormor" is your mother's mother. Danish has a separate word for each grandparent, so you can tell which side of the family you mean: "mor" (mother) plus "mor" (mother) gives "mormor". Your father's mother is "farmor". Children often say "mormor" like a name.

sentence.en: My grandmother lives in Aarhus.

en mund.explanation: "En mund" is a mouth. It is an en-word. You will often hear it in the saying "Hold munden!" (Be quiet!), which is rude, and in "Luk munden op" (Open your mouth), which is what a dentist says. Learn it together with "tand" and "tunge".

sentence.en: Open your mouth, please.

en mus.explanation: "En mus" is a mouse, and it is an en-word. The plural is the same as the singular, so "to mus" means two mice. You also use it for the computer mouse, so "en computermus" is the thing you click with. A rat is "en rotte".

sentence.da: Der løber en **mus** hen over gulvet.
sentence.en: A mouse runs across the floor.

en måde.explanation: "En måde" is a way of doing something, and it is an en-word. "På den måde" means in that way, and "på en eller anden måde" means somehow. Do not mix it up with a road or path, which is "en vej". The plural is "måder".

sentence.da: Det kan man gøre på mange **måder**.
sentence.en: You can do that in many ways.

en måne.explanation: En måne is a moon. In daily life you mostly say "månen" (the moon), as in "Månen er stor i aften". The word is an en-word. Be careful not to mix it up with "en måned", which means a month. They look alike and share a start, but they mean different things, and only "måned" is about the calendar.

sentence.en: The moon is big tonight.

en måned.explanation: "Måned" is the ordinary word for a month. Months of the year are written with a small letter in Danish (januar, februar), unlike in English. You will often hear "om måneden" meaning "per month", for example when talking about rent or pay.

sentence.en: I pay rent every month.

et marked.explanation: Et marked is a market, such as an open-air place where people sell fruit, vegetables or second-hand things. It is an et-word, so "the market" is "markedet". "Et loppemarked" is a flea market. The same word is also used for the economy side of things, for example when people talk about "markedet" in the news.

sentence.en: We buy vegetables at the market.

et mellemnavn.explanation: "Et mellemnavn" is a middle name, one that sits between the first and last name. "Mellem" means "between". Many Danes have one, and it is often an old family name. Some forms ask for it, but you can leave it empty if you have none.

sentence.en: I do not have a middle name.

et menneske.explanation: "Et menneske" is a human being, and it is an et-word, even though it refers to a person. The plural "mennesker" is the common word for "people" in everyday speech: "mange mennesker" means lots of people. Use it when speaking about people in general.

sentence.en: There are many people in town.

et menukort.explanation: "Et menukort" is the menu in a restaurant, the list of dishes and drinks. It is an et-word, so "the menu" is "menukortet". You can ask a waiter "Må jeg se menukortet?" (May I see the menu?). People also say "en menu" for a set meal with several courses.

sentence.en: Can I see the menu, please?

et minut.explanation: Et minut is a minute, 60 seconds. It is an et-word, which can be surprising for English speakers, so remember "et minut" and "minuttet" (the minute). More than one is "minutter". People often ask others to wait with "Vent et øjeblik" (wait a moment), but "Vent et minut" is also fine.

sentence.en: Wait a minute, please.

et museum.explanation: Et museum is a museum, a place with art, history or science to look at. It is an et-word, and it behaves in a special way: for "the museum" the end "-um" is dropped and you get "museet", and for more than one you get "museer". You say "på museet" for "at the museum".

sentence.en: We are visiting the museum today.

et måltid.explanation: "Et måltid" is a meal, any occasion when you sit down to eat, like breakfast, lunch or dinner. It is an et-word. In Danish people also use "et måltid mad" (a meal of food). It is built from "mål" (a set time) and "tid" (time).

sentence.en: The most important meal of the day is breakfast.

et møde.explanation: "Et møde" is a meeting, and it is an et-word. The plural is "møder". It comes from the verb "at møde", to meet. "Jeg har et møde klokken ti" means "I have a meeting at ten". For meeting a person by chance you can also say "at møde nogen".

sentence.en: We have a meeting tomorrow.

mad.explanation: "Mad" means food, in general. It is an en-word and is used for what you eat, as a whole. You say "Jeg elsker dansk mad". For one dish Danish uses "en ret" (a dish), and "en mad" can mean a sandwich.

sentence.en: I like Danish food.

maj.explanation: "Maj" is May. It is a short word that sounds like English "my", and it is written with a small letter. You say "i maj" for in May. It is a lovely month in Denmark, with the first warm days and several public holidays.

sentence.en: We are going on vacation in May.

majs.explanation: "Majs" is corn, the yellow kind that you eat as a vegetable. It is an en-word and is not counted, so you say "noget majs". A whole ear is "en majskolbe", and "popcorn" is the snack made from it. It is often sold in cans and used in salads.

sentence.en: I want corn in the salad.

man.explanation: "Man" means "one" or "you" in the general sense of people, anyone. It is very common in Danish, much more than "one" is in English, for rules and tips. Do not confuse it with "en mand" (a man) or "du" (you, a specific person).

sentence.en: You may not park here.

mandag.explanation: Monday is the start of the Danish working week. Use "på mandag" for "on Monday" (next one) and "om mandagen" for "on Mondays" in general. Day names are written with a small letter in Danish, unlike in English. A tip: "i mandags" means last Monday.

sentence.en: I am off on Monday.

mandlig.explanation: "Mandlig" means male or masculine. It comes from "mand" (man). You will see it on forms, for example when asked about sex, and in job descriptions. The opposite is "kvindelig". Note the extra -t with et-words: "et mandligt navn".

sentence.en: He is a male nurse.

mange.explanation: "Mange" means "many" and is used for things you can count: "mange biler" (many cars). It never changes. The question "Hvor mange?" means "How many?". For things you cannot count, like water or time, use "meget" instead.

sentence.en: There are many people here.

forms.en: Thank you very much for the help.

mange tak.explanation: "Mange tak" means "many thanks" and is a bit stronger than plain "tak". Add "for" and the thing you are thankful for. It is polite and useful in shops, restaurants and with strangers. The reply is "selv tak" or "ingen årsag".

sentence.en: Thank you very much for the gift!

marts.explanation: "Marts" is March. Notice that it ends in -s, which is easy to forget, and it is written with a small letter. You say "i marts" for in March. Danes often use it with dates: "den tiende marts" is the tenth of March.

sentence.en: Spring begins in March.

masser af.explanation: "Masser af" means lots of, a large amount of something. It is informal and common in everyday talk, and it works with both things you can count and things you cannot. "Masser" does not change, and "af" is always followed by the thing: "masser af mad" (lots of food).

sentence.da: Der er **masser af** mad i køleskabet.
sentence.en: There is lots of food in the fridge.

matematik.explanation: "Matematik" means maths (math), the school lesson or the topic in general. It is an en-word and you use it without "en" in front. In school talk Danes often shorten it to "matte". Say "Jeg er god til matematik" for "I am good at math".

sentence.en: I have math at nine o'clock.

mayonnaise.explanation: "Mayonnaise" is mayonnaise, and it is an en-word. It is usually said as "mayo" in everyday talk, and in Denmark it is common on open sandwiches and with fries. It is not counted, so you say "noget mayonnaise". Its spelling is tricky, so learn it as a whole.

sentence.da: Jeg vil have lidt **mayonnaise** på brødet.
sentence.en: I want a little mayonnaise on the bread.

forms.en: a cup of coffee with milk

med.explanation: "Med" means with. It is also a small word meaning along: "tage med" is to take along or go along, and "komme med" is to come along. The opposite is "uden" (without).

related.en: to take along, to go along

sentence.en: I live with my brother.

med det samme.explanation: "Med det samme" means "right away" or "immediately". It literally says "with the same", but just learn it as a fixed phrase. It goes at the end of a sentence, like "jeg kommer med det samme". For something slightly softer, "om lidt" means "in a little while".

sentence.da: Jeg ringer til dig **med det samme**.
sentence.en: I'll call you right away.

medicin.explanation: "Medicin" is medicine, the drugs you take when you are sick. It is an en-word. You say "at tage medicin" (to take medicine), and "medicinen" when you mean the specific one. It is often used with "recept" (a prescription) at the pharmacy.

sentence.en: I take my medicine every morning.

forms.en: I have a lot of time.

meget.explanation: "Meget" means "very" in front of a describing word, as in "meget god" (very good), and "a lot" or "much" with amounts, as in "meget vand" (a lot of water). It is also used alone: "Tak for meget" is a way to say a big thank you. For things you can count, Danes use "mange" (many) instead. A tip: "meget" never changes its ending.

sentence.en: It is very cold today.

mel.explanation: "Mel" is flour, and it is an et-word, so "the flour" is "melet". It is not counted, so you say "noget mel" or "to dl mel" (two decilitres of flour). It is used for baking bread and cakes, and for thickening sauces. Short and simple to spell, but don't mix it up with "mælk" (milk).

sentence.en: We need flour for the cake.

forms.en: between the house and the forest

mellem.explanation: "Mellem" means between, and it is used for places, times and amounts. It often goes with "og" (and): "mellem to og tre". It is also used for "among two or more", like "forskellen mellem dem" (the difference between them).

sentence.en: The bank is between the post office and the school.

men.explanation: "Men" means but, and it joins two ideas that go against each other. It is one of the most common words in Danish and very easy to use. After "men", the sentence continues with the normal word order: "Jeg er træt, men jeg kommer".

sentence.en: I am tired, but I am coming.

mens.explanation: "Mens" means while, and it joins two things that happen at the same time. After "mens", the doer comes first: "mens jeg venter". A close friend is "imens", which means "meanwhile". It is very common when telling a story or describing a daily routine.

sentence.en: I drink coffee while I read.

mere.explanation: "Mere" means "more" and is used for amounts you cannot count, like "mere vand" or "mere tid". Put it before a describing word to make a comparison: "mere interessant" (more interesting). "Ikke mere" means "no longer" or "no more". For things you can count, "flere" is the usual word.

sentence.en: Can I have more coffee?

mest.explanation: "Mest" means "most" or "mostly". "Mest af alt" means "most of all". Put it before a describing word to say the top level, like "mest interessant" (most interesting). The pattern is "mere" (more), then "mest" (most).

sentence.en: I like coffee the most.

mig.explanation: "Mig" means "me". You use it when something is done to you, or after words like "til" and "med". When you are the one doing it, you say "jeg" instead. The Danish for "with me" is "med mig", and "to me" is "til mig".

sentence.en: Can you help me?

million.explanation: "En million" is a million. It is an en-word, so you say "en million" for one, and add -er for more: "to millioner" (two million). After a number, the thing counted goes after "million": "en million mennesker" (a million people). Do not mix it up with "milliard", which means a billion (1,000 million).

sentence.da: Der bor over fem **millioner** mennesker i Danmark.
sentence.en: More than five million people live in Denmark.

min.explanation: "Min" means "my" or "mine" and goes with en-words, such as "min bil" (my car) or "min ven" (my friend). For et-words use "mit", and for many things "mine". It comes before the thing, just like in English, and in Danish it does not take "the" with it.

sentence.en: My mother lives in Odense.

mindre.explanation: "Mindre" means both less (an amount) and smaller (a size). It is the "more small" form of "lille" and "lidt", which is why one word covers both ideas. The opposite is "mere" for more amount or "større" for bigger size.

sentence.en: I eat less bread now.

mine.explanation: "Mine" means "my" or "mine" when you talk about more than one thing, such as "mine børn" (my children). It works for both en-words and et-words, so you do not have to choose. For one thing you use "min" or "mit" instead.

sentence.en: Those are my keys.

mit.explanation: "Mit" means "my" or "mine" and goes with et-words, such as "mit hus" (my house) or "mit navn" (my name). For en-words you say "min", and for many things "mine". A good tip is to learn each word together with en or et, so you know which one to pick.

sentence.en: That is my house.

mod.explanation: "Mod" means against or toward, depending on the sentence. It can mean opposing something ("imod" is often used for that) or heading in a direction ("mod nord"). As a different word, "et mod" means courage. A tip: "Jeg er imod" is the common way to say "I am against it".

sentence.en: We are walking toward the station.

morgenmad.explanation: "Morgenmad" is breakfast, built from "morgen" (morning) and "mad" (food). It is an en-word, and you say "til morgenmad" for "for breakfast". To eat it, you use "at spise morgenmad". Notice that no "a" is needed: "Jeg spiser morgenmad".

sentence.en: We eat breakfast at seven o'clock.

musik.explanation: "Musik" means music. It is an en-word and is used without "en" when you mean music in general. You listen to it: "at lytte til musik". For a lesson at school you say "Jeg har musik". A musician is "en musiker".

sentence.en: I love music.

må jeg bede om regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg bede om regningen?" is a very polite way to ask for the bill at a restaurant. "Må jeg bede om" means "may I ask for". A shorter, normal way is "regningen, tak". "Regning" is an en-word, so it becomes "regningen" with "the" on the end.

sentence.da: **Må jeg bede om regningen?** Vi skal af sted.
sentence.en: May I have the bill? We have to go.

forms.da: Må jeg få en kop kaffe?
forms.en: May I have a cup of coffee?

må jeg få regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg få regningen?" means "May I have the bill?" and is polite to say in a restaurant or café. "Må jeg få ...?" is a general polite way to ask for something, so you can use it for "menuen" (the menu) or "en kop kaffe" (a cup of coffee). "Regningen" is "the bill", which is "en regning" plus the ending "-en" for "the". Danes often say "tak" afterwards.

sentence.en: May I have the bill, please?

måske.explanation: "Måske" means "maybe" or "perhaps" and shows that you are not sure. When it starts a sentence, the verb comes next, as in "Måske kommer han" (Maybe he will come). In the middle of the sentence, it goes after the verb, as in "Han kommer måske". A tip: it is a good, polite answer when you don't want to say yes or no right away.

sentence.en: Maybe he will come tomorrow.

mælk.explanation: "Mælk" means milk. It is an en-word, so "the milk" is "mælken". It takes no "a" in front: you say "Jeg drikker mælk". For quantity use "et glas mælk" (a glass of milk) or "en liter mælk" (a litre of milk).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **mælk** hver morgen.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of milk every morning.

mæt.explanation: "Mæt" means full after eating, with no more room for food. "Jeg er mæt" is the polite way to say you have had enough, and you can use it to refuse seconds. It already ends in "t", so it stays the same for en-words and et-words, and the form for more than one is "mætte". The opposite is "sulten". Do not use it to say a room is full; for that use "fuld".

sentence.en: Thank you, I am full.

mørk.explanation: "Mørk" means dark, for light, rooms, nights and colours: "mørkeblå" is dark blue. Danes also use it for dark hair and dark chocolate. Add "t" for et-words ("et mørkt rum") and "-e" for more than one. The word "mørke" is the darkness itself, as in "i mørket" (in the dark). The opposite is "lys" (light, bright).

sentence.en: It is very dark outside.

mørkeblå.explanation: "Mørkeblå" means dark blue or navy. It is made from "mørk" (dark) and "blå" (blue) joined into one word. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et mørkeblåt tørklæde"), and with more than one it stays "mørkeblå".

sentence.en: My jacket is dark blue.

mørkegrøn.explanation: "Mørkegrøn" means dark green. It is made of "mørk" (dark) and "grøn" (green) joined into one word. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et mørkegrønt hus") and with more than one "ne" ("mørkegrønne biler"). The lighter one is "lysegrøn".

sentence.en: My jacket is dark green.

müsli.explanation: "Müsli" is muesli, the breakfast mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit. It is an en-word, but is normally used without "en": "Jeg spiser müsli". Note the letter "ü", which is kept from the original word, though Danes often write it as "musli" too.

sentence.en: I eat muesli for breakfast.
